items.prompt: A batch of unsorted event codes must be emitted as (code, count) groups in ascending code order. Which representation makes each group processable with one forward pass?
constraints: The output explicitly requires ascending code order.
Equal codes use ordinary exact equality.

options.text: Keep input order and treat only currently adjacent equal codes as one group.
Sort codes by their unknown final frequency before counting them.
Sort by code, then process each maximal equal-code run.
Compare each code with every later code and emit a group after each comparison.

feedback.reason: Sorting by the grouping key makes every equality class one contiguous run and already supplies the requested output order.

blocks.text: A maximal run begins when the current code differs from the previous one and ends just before the next different code. Because all equal keys are contiguous after sorting, the pass can count and emit each group exactly once. Input adjacency does not capture separated occurrences, while sorting by frequency is circular because frequency is the value being computed rather than an available key.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.input_adjacent_runs: Separated occurrences of the same code would become multiple incomplete groups.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_by_count: The frequency is not known before grouping, and it is not the key that defines membership.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.pair_every_code: Pairwise comparison repeats work and does not naturally produce one maximal group per code.

items.prompt: Order the core state transitions while scanning a nonempty array that has already been sorted by the grouping key.
constraints: The loop visits items from left to right.
This ordering covers a key change inside the loop; final end-of-input flushing is handled separately.

elements.text: Compare the next item's key with currentKey.
Increment count on equality; otherwise emit the completed run.
After emitting on a key change, set currentKey to the new key and reset count to one.
Initialize currentKey and count from the first sorted item.

feedback.reason: The next key is interpreted relative to initialized run state, and a new run starts only after the prior one is emitted.

blocks.text: The scan maintains one invariant: currentKey and count describe exactly the current equal-key run through the previously consumed item. The update then branches on the next key.

items: For a nonempty input, initialize currentKey from the first item and count = 1.
Read the next item and compare its grouping key with currentKey.
If the keys are equal, increment count and continue; otherwise emit (currentKey, count) before overwriting either value.
Only on the key-change branch, set currentKey to the new key and reset count = 1.

blocks.title: The loop cannot flush the last run
blocks.text: After all items are consumed, emit the retained (currentKey, count) once more because no later unequal key triggers the change branch.

items.prompt: A sorted run scanner emits a group only when it sees a different next key. For input [2, 2, 5, 5, 5], which defect remains after the loop ends?
constraints: There is no artificial sentinel appended to the array.

options.text: The run for key 2 can never be counted because it is first.
Sorting deletes the repeated 5 values.
No action is needed because end of input acts as an automatic key change.
The run for key 5 remains in state and must be emitted after the loop.

feedback.reason: The final run has no following key change to trigger emission, so it requires an explicit post-loop flush.

blocks.text: The scanner's transition rule emits a run when it encounters the first element of the next run. The last run has no such element, even though its count is correct in memory. End of iteration is control flow, not an implicit data key. A sentinel can encode the same boundary if it is guaranteed not to collide and is handled deliberately, but the stated implementation has none.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.first_run_not_counted: The first run is initialized from the first item and is emitted when key 5 appears.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorting_removed_fives: Sorting reorders occurrences; it does not delete multiplicity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_runs_already_emitted: Loop termination does not execute the key-change branch, so the retained final state is not output automatically.

items.prompt: Records must be grouped by category in ascending category order. For each category, output the earliest timestamp record; timestamp ties require the smallest record ID. Which sorted-run design makes the first record of each run the required representative?
constraints: Every category has at least one record.

options.text: Sort by (category, timestamp, recordId), then take the first record of each category run.
Sort by category only and take whichever record appears first in each run.
Sort by timestamp only and treat adjacent timestamps as categories.
Sort category descending and timestamp descending, then take each run's first record.

feedback.reason: The first-in-run shortcut is correct only when the full sort key encodes both representative tie-breaks inside each category.

blocks.text: Category as the primary key creates the group boundary. Timestamp then orders candidate representatives from earliest to latest, and record ID resolves equal timestamps deterministically. A category-only sort guarantees contiguity but not which member appears first. The distinction matters because grouping membership and representative selection are separate contracts that happen to be implemented by one composite order here.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.category_only: It forms correct runs but leaves the chosen representative dependent on prior order or sort stability.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.time_only: Timestamp order can interleave categories, so equal-category records are not guaranteed to form one run.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.category_desc_time_desc: This reverses both required category output order and earliest-record selection.

items.prompt: A report groups equal values after sorting and must list the original positions belonging to each group. Select all required preservation steps.
constraints: Equal values may occur many times.
Positions inside each output group must be ascending original indices.

options.text: Within each completed value run, order or collect original indices according to the output contract.
Treat the positions inside the sorted array as original positions.
Keep only the run count and reconstruct all source positions later from the value.
Attach originalIndex to every occurrence before sorting.

feedback.reason: Grouping by value does not preserve source positions automatically; occurrence identity must be carried and then emitted in the required index order.

blocks.text: Decorating each occurrence preserves which source element entered a run. Sorting by value establishes run membership, but it may not order original indices inside the run unless index is included as a tie-break or the run's indices are separately normalized. Sorted positions are coordinates in the transformed array. A count records multiplicity but cannot reconstruct the exact member identities requested by the report.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.use_sorted_positions: Sorted coordinates change after reordering and do not name the source occurrences.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.store_count_only: Multiplicity alone loses which original positions contributed to the group, especially with repeated values.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.attach_index: Each occurrence needs a stable source identity before sorting can move it into a run.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.order_group_indices: The output's intra-group index order is a separate requirement that must be enforced explicitly.

items.prompt: The task is to return an unordered map from each string to its frequency. Expected O(n) hashing is permitted, and no sorted output is required. Which assessment is correct?
constraints: The input strings are immutable keys with a valid hash implementation.

options.text: Equal strings can be counted only after sorting makes them adjacent.
Accumulate frequencies in a hash map; sorting is a valid alternative but not automatically better.
Every string must be compared with every other string because output is grouped.
Comparison sorting is expected O(n), so it dominates hashing.

feedback.reason: Direct keyed aggregation already creates the required groups without paying for an unused total order.

blocks.text: A frequency map represents one accumulator per equality class and processes each occurrence once under the stated expected hash model. Sort-then-runs is still useful when ordered output, low auxiliary memory under an in-place sort, or deterministic comparison behaviour is required. None of those benefits appears in this contract, so grouping does not itself prove that sorting is the preferred mechanism.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_required: Hash keys group separated equal strings through shared map state; adjacency is not the only complete mechanism.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.quadratic_required: The map avoids pairwise comparisons by directly locating the accumulator for each key.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_is_expected_linear: Generic comparison sorting is O(n log n), not expected O(n), under the stated model.

items.prompt: A comparison sort arranges n records by group key, then one pass emits each maximal equal-key run. What is the tightest offered worst-case total time bound?
constraints: The comparison sort has worst-case Θ(n log n) time.
Emitting aggregate metadata is O(1) per input record in total.

feedback.reason: Run processing is linear, but comparison sorting remains the asymptotically dominant phase.

blocks.text: The scan advances through each record once and performs constant aggregate work, giving Θ(n). Adding it to the stated Θ(n log n) comparison sort gives Θ(n log n + n) = Θ(n log n), matching the offered O(n log n) bound. The number of distinct groups does not remove sorting cost.

blocks.title: Why the other offered bounds are wrong
blocks.text: O(n) ignores comparison sorting. O(n²) is a loose upper bound, not the tightest offered bound; neither sorting nor the one-pass run scan performs quadratic pairwise work. A bounded-key counting arrangement could be linear, but it is a different declared algorithm.

items.prompt: Select all designs where sorting by the stated key guarantees that every intended equivalence class forms one contiguous run.
constraints: The intended group relation is exactly the one described in each option.
extractedDay uses one specified timezone for every timestamp.

options.text: Group words case-insensitively by sorting on caseFold(word) and testing equality of that same normalized key.
Group words case-insensitively after sorting only by their raw case-sensitive spelling.
Group timestamps by calendar day by sorting on extractedDay(timestamp) and testing that same day key.
Group anagrams after sorting only by string length.

feedback.reason: Contiguous runs are guaranteed when the primary sort key is the same deterministic key that defines group equality.

blocks.text: Case-folded text and extracted calendar day each produce a canonical group key; sorting by that key places all equal keys together. Raw spelling can interleave case-insensitive equivalents with other strings, and length alone coarsens many non-anagram strings into one region without making each anagram signature contiguous. A secondary tie-break may order members inside a run, but the group key must remain primary.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.raw_sort_casefold_group: Case-sensitive order does not guarantee that every case-insensitive equivalent occupies one uninterrupted block.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.length_sort_anagram_group: Equal length is necessary for anagrams but not the equivalence key, so different signatures can interleave the intended groups.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.casefold_words: The normalized case-folded key is both the sort key and the equality key, guaranteeing one run per class.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.date_day: Extracted day identity directly defines the groups and therefore becomes contiguous under the same primary key.

items.prompt: After sorting values, how should a scan identify one maximal run of equal values?

options.text: Keep advancing while the next value equals the run's representative, then process the half-open run boundary.
Compare each value with a random earlier value in the array.
Stop immediately when a neighboring value equals the current one.
Resort the remaining suffix before every group.

feedback.reason: Sorted order makes equal values contiguous, so one forward boundary scan captures the entire run.

blocks.text: Using a half-open interval [start,end) makes the next scan begin exactly at end and prevents double-processing or skipping the first different value.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.compare_random: Random positions do not reveal contiguous equality runs.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.stop_first_equal: The first equal neighbor proves the run continues rather than ends.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.resort_each_run: The initial sort already provides the needed adjacency.

items.prompt: What does the length of a maximal equal-value run represent after sorting?

options.text: The frequency of that value in the input.
The original index of the first occurrence, even after values were rearranged.
The total number of distinct values in the array.
The sum of all values outside the run.

feedback.reason: Sorting places every occurrence of a value adjacent, so its run length equals its multiplicity.

blocks.text: The run length can feed a frequency, compression, duplicate-detection, or grouped-processing result. Original positions require carrying provenance separately.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.first_index: Sorting changes positions unless original indices were stored as payload.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.distinct_count: One run represents one distinct value, not all distinct values.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.range_sum: Run length counts entries; it does not sum values outside the run.

items.prompt: How is a frequency obtained from one equal-value run after sorting?

options.text: Use the run length end-start for a half-open run [start,end).
Subtract the value from its first index.
Use the full array length for every run.
Use the total number of distinct values.

feedback.reason: Contiguous equal entries occupy exactly the run's half-open span.

blocks.text: The next scan begins at end, so every sorted entry is counted once. A run length is multiplicity, not the numeric value itself.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.value-minus-index: Value magnitude does not determine occurrence count.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.global-length: Different values can have different frequencies.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.number-of-keys: That counts groups, not members of one group.

items.prompt: After processing a sorted equal-value run [start,end), where should the next run scan begin?

options.text: At end, the first index not included in the completed run.
At start, which would process the same run again.
At end+1, which can skip the next value.
Always restart at index zero.

feedback.reason: Half-open boundaries make end the exact next unprocessed position.

blocks.text: This convention prevents both duplicate processing and skipped values, including at the final run ending at n.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.end-plus-one: It can skip a distinct value immediately after the run.

items.prompt: How should a singleton value appear in a sorted run-processing algorithm?

options.text: As a run whose end is start+1 and whose frequency is one.
Skip it because grouping only concerns duplicates.
Merge it with adjacent unequal values.
Assign frequency zero because it has no duplicate.

feedback.reason: Every distinct value forms a group, even when its multiplicity is one.

blocks.text: The output may later filter singleton groups if it asks only for duplicates, but the scan must first represent them correctly to maintain coverage.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.skip-singleton: Skipping can lose distinct values or shift the next boundary.

items.prompt: What does a grouped output need to retain when the task asks for all members of each equal-key group?

options.text: The key and the full collection of records mapped to it.
Only one key per group, with members discarded.
Only the last record encountered for each key.
One count for the entire input, regardless of key.

feedback.reason: A grouped output is a partition of records, so each bucket must preserve its members or the requested summary.

blocks.text: Sorting gives contiguous runs; a map or output segment can retain the complete group. Key-only state is sufficient only for a distinct-key output.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.global-count: One aggregate cannot represent per-key groups.
